NORTHERN VIRGINIA ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE, INC. TO MOTION FOR LEAVE
      TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF PJM INTERCONNECTION, L.L.C.

         Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal

Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or the “Commission”),1 Northern Virginia Electric

Cooperative, Inc. (“NOVEC”) respectfully submits this motion for leave to answer and answer to

PJM Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) motion for leave to answer and answer (“PJM Answer”)2

to NOVEC’s August 21, 2026, protest (“NOVEC Protest”)3 of the July 31, 2026, filing by PJM

to revise its Open Access Transmission Tariff (“Tariff”) and Reliability Assurance Agreement

Among Load Serving Entities (“RAA”) to establish the Reliability Backstop Procurement

(“RBP”).4

         For the reasons set forth herein and in the NOVEC Protest, the Commission should reject

the RBP as unjust and unreasonable. If the Commission does not reject the RBP, it should

require revisions on compliance to eliminate or substantially reduce the nearly $2 billion

collateral requirement that the RBP Proposal would impose on NOVEC, or set the collateral

requirement for settlement and hearing judge procedures as suggested by PJM.5

                              I.       MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER

          NOVEC respectfully requests leave to submit this answer. The Commission regularly

allows answers for good cause shown, such as when the answers help ensure a more accurate and

complete record, clarify the issues, or provide useful and relevant information that will assist the

Commission in its deliberative process.6 This answer will correct PJM’s mischaracterizations of

the context of the RBP framework, the unjust and unreasonable character of the RBP proposal,

and the need to substantially revise PJM’s proposed collateral requirements for the Load Serving

Entities (“LSE”) RBP Buyers. In addition, this answer provides useful and relevant information

that will assist the Commission in its deliberative process. To the extent that this answer does not

address an issue raised in PJM’s answer, that should not be construed as agreement with PJM.

    II.     ANSWER TO PJM’S ANSWER TO THE PROTESTS AND COMMENTS ON
                               THE RBP PROPOSAL

     A. Mr. Coscia’s Supplemental Affidavit explains the many flaws in PJM’s proposed

        purpose and fundamentally onerous and not just or reasonable.

out that the amount of collateral should be related to the risk that an LSE fails to pay an RBP

Charge and PJM’s methodology does not secure against that loss because it is focused on the risk

that a large load fails to materialize.9 Mr. Coscia challenges PJM’s use of a uniform Credit

     B. The capacity shortfall experienced by PJM resulted from a combination of causes in
        addition to growth of large customer load.

        PJM recognized in its original filing that the capacity shortfall it is seeking to address is

the result of many causes, stating that “it is well-documented and recognized that supply and

demand in the PJM Region have converged, as a significant portion of PJM’s thermal generation

fleet have retired while replacement resources are arriving at a slower pace than the

unprecedented load growth” and “[t]ogether, these factors have strained the RPM Auction’s

ability to procure sufficient capacity to meet the PJM Region Reliability Requirement in recent

capacity auctions.”14 Despite the other causes, PJM in answering NOVEC now maintains that

“[t]he entire PJM Region is facing a capacity shortfall because entities like NOVEC contracted

        First, NOVEC does not have any control over which customers receive electric service.

Nor does NOVEC have a say in which customers choose to site in NOVEC’s service territory.

NOVEC has an obligation under state law to serve its load, and NOVEC follows state law.

        Second, unlike Regional Transmission Organizations (“RTO”) like the Midcontinent

Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”), where the capacity market is a backup mechanism

and LSEs are primarily responsible for meeting their resource adequacy requirements through

bilateral arrangements,16 in PJM the Reliability Pricing Model (“RPM”) is the primary

mechanism for LSEs to procure capacity. The Base Residual Auction in the RPM may allow

LSEs to bilaterally contract for their capacity needs,17 but PJM operates the RPM to “ensure that

enough capacity is procured, at a reasonable cost, to maintain reliable grid operations” and the

rules do not indicate a maximum amount that LSEs can receive from PJM’s relevant capacity

auctions.18

requirement for an LSE to bring its own new capacity.19 There is no basis for PJM’s criticism

     C. The Commission should exercise its authority under NRG to require PJM to adopt
        the voluntary RBP framework approved in the stakeholder process, or in the
        alternative, reject the RBP Proposal with guidance on filing a voluntary iteration.

        The Commission should exercise its authority under NRG to require PJM to revise its

would not work. PJM contends that “a voluntary, subscription-based framework would not

quo”22 and that under the status quo, LSEs have not entered into bilateral agreements.23 PJM’s

observation that LSEs have not entered into bilateral agreements prior to the filing of the RBP is

immaterial and irrelevant. As NOVEC explained above, the RPM does not depend on bilateral

        The imposition of a voluntary process would also eliminate the contradiction of PJM’s

opt-out mechanism. As Mr. Coscia explains in his supplemental affidavit, PJM justifies its opt-

out provision as addressing a limited regulatory gap faced by non-public utilities whose rates are

not regulated by the states.32 In its answer, PJM argues that those customers are at the risk of an

that one Virginia cooperative, Old Dominion Electric Cooperative, could opt out but another,

customers may still have to absorb the cost of an overbuy notwithstanding state regulation.35 Mr.

Coscia opines that “the economic rationale for the opt-out would be stronger if eligibility tracked

the overbuy risk PJM identifies rather than state rate-regulatory status standing alone.”36

NOVEC would support either. The Commission could extend the opt-out to all non-public

utilities in recognition of the presence of the overbuy risk. Or the Commission could require PJM

to adopt the voluntary, subscription-based RBP framework which would give all utilities and

their customers the ability to manage their own exposure. The voluntary RBP framework

eliminates the need for an opt-out by allowing utilities and their customers to enter arrangements

that can effectively manage any overbuy risk.

      E. The collateral requirement is unjust and unreasonable because it is duplicative,
        excessive, and the initial credit rate is insupportably high. The collateral

             a. The collateral requirement is subjective, unduly discriminatory, and unjust
                and unreasonable because it is excessive.

        PJM’s proposed collateral requirement is not just and reasonable. PJM asserts that its

methodology strikes an appropriate balance between protecting PJM’s markets and ensuring

market participants have adequate flexibility to manage their collateral requirements.55 PJM

notes that the Commission has cautioned against overly conservative credit requirements that are

poorly correlated to credit risk that would impose costs.56 PJM’s methodology does not strike

that balance.

        As a threshold matter, not even PJM can reasonably claim that its proposal ensures

market participants have adequate flexibility to manage their collateral requirements. Market

participants have no flexibility to manage their collateral requirements. They must post the full

amount, with no exceptions for individual credit risk and subject only to intermittent and

irregular reductions at PJM’s discretion.57 PJM has set the obligation so high for NOVEC that

SUPPLEMENTAL REPLY AFFIDAVIT OF CARL F. COSCIA, Ph.D.
On Behalf of Northern Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc.


I. PURPOSE, POSTURE, AND PRINCIPAL CONCLUSIONS
  1.   My name is Carl F. Coscia. I am the Principal of Toller Energy. I submitted an
       affidavit in this docket on August 21, 2026 in support of the Protest of Northern
       Virginia Electric Cooperative, Inc. (“NOVEC”) (“NOVEC Coscia Aff.”).1 My
       qualifications, the basis for my opinions, and the materials I reviewed are set out

       are my own. No part of my compensation is contingent on the outcome of this
       proceeding.

  1.   Since submitting that affidavit, I have reviewed the Motion for Leave to Answer and

     percent is $1,519,312.50 per MW. The filed $1.5 million figure is therefore
     approximately 49.4 percent of that gross amount. But the RBP does not settle as a
     single fifteen-year payment at inception. Load pays the RPM clearing price through
     ordinary capacity settlement and pays or receives the difference between the RBP
     commitment price and the RPM clearing price through the RBP settlement
     mechanism.
  12. Gross contractual value therefore is not itself a measure of loss on default. The
     relevant credit exposure depends on when a default occurs, what amounts remain
     payable, what RPM prices have been established, what collateral has already been
     posted and applied, what amounts are reallocated under section 18.9(a), and what
     residual, if any, reaches the broader PJM membership.

 13. PJM’s Answer describes that default consequence in two ways. In responding to
     EKPC, PJM states that an unpaid RBP Charge is reallocated among other LSEs
     already responsible for RBP Charges. PJM Answer at 67 n.205. In defending the
     magnitude of the credit requirement, PJM states that the approach “balances the
     protection of Members against the effects of LSE default,” citing Operating
     Agreement section 15.2.2. Id. at 84 & n.252. Those provisions may describe
     successive levels of a default waterfall. Their relationship determines the residual
     loss. See EKPC Reply Aff. ¶¶ 18–24.
 14. PJM addressed the same question during the stakeholder process. Its April 2026
     design presentation states, under the heading “Default Allocation,” that “[i]f a
     default occurs as a result of a nonpayment of a RBP charge, that amount would be
     handled as a default allocation assessment under the existing OA Section 15.2.2,”
     and described that treatment as consistent with the existing RPM market. April 17
     Design Presentation at 47. That statement indicates that unpaid RBP Charges were
     expected to reach the broader membership through the same mechanism that
     applies to other market defaults.

 15. NOVEC carries approximately nineteen percent of the Initial RBP Target. Its original
     affidavit explained that a failure to post collateral or a payment default at that scale
     would not remain confined to the cooperative. NOVEC Coscia Aff. ¶¶ 14(h), 68–69.
     The size of the residual loss, and who bears it, therefore should be identified before
     the amount of collateral intended to absorb it is selected.
 16. In my opinion, a formula based on approximately one-half of gross contractual value
     does not establish that relationship. Additional procedures should first define what
     remains unpaid after the RBP settlement, collateral application, section 18.9(a)
     reallocation, and any Operating Agreement section 15.2.2 allocation. Only then can a
     buyer-side Credit Rate be evaluated against the loss it is intended to secure.



III. PJM’S CREDIT-MIGRATION ANALYSIS DOES NOT SUPPORT A UNIFORM RATE
 17. PJM defends a Credit Rate that does not vary with an obligor’s credit condition in
     part by reference to credit migration. PJM extrapolates a ten-year S&P Global
     corporate rating-transition study to fifteen years and reasons that an individualized
     credit approach could require additional collateral as an LSE’s creditworthiness
     deteriorates. PJM Answer at 81–83 & Table 2.
 18. Credit migration over a fifteen-year horizon is a legitimate credit consideration. But
    the fact that credit quality can change supports periodic measurement and
    adjustment; it does not explain why the obligor’s credit condition should be ignored.

19. NOVEC illustrates the problem. Assuming an annual carrying cost of 100 basis
    points, the requirement would cost approximately $19.5 million per year,
    approximately 94 percent of NOVEC’s 2025 patronage capital and operating
    margins. At 150, 200, and 300 basis points, the carrying cost rises to approximately
    141, 188, and 281 percent of that margin, respectively. Mr. Rollins further explains
    the consequences for NOVEC’s credit rating, its ability to transact bilaterally, and its
    capacity to borrow for infrastructure. Rollins Aff. at 3:7-20.

20. A generalized corporate transition matrix does not measure the effect of imposing
    collateral comparable to or exceeding an obligor’s balance sheet. A requirement of
    that magnitude can consume liquidity, encumber assets, absorb credit-facility
    capacity, and impose recurring financing expense. The requirement can therefore
    affect the very credit quality the migration analysis is used to predict. EKPC Reply
    Aff. ¶¶ 25–30.

21. PJM already has current, participant-specific information concerning NOVEC. PJM
    bills NOVEC, observes its payment performance, measures exposure under
    Attachment Q, monitors internal and external credit ratings, and receives financial
    information through its existing credit processes. NOVEC Coscia Aff. ¶¶ 25–27. At
    December 31, 2025, NOVEC reported approximately $34.4 million of cash collateral
    posted to PJM against its existing market activity. Id.

22. The proposed RBP requirement changes that result by a factor of approximately 57.
    The original affidavit compared approximately $34.4 million of existing PJM
    collateral with approximately $1.954 billion of incremental RBP collateral. Id. ¶¶
    10(d), 27.

23. PJM also uses a term-sensitive methodology on the seller side of the same RBP
    construct. The seller requirement is tied to a defined period of exposure, is
    discounted, declines as the commitment runs off, and permits reductions that take
    account of participant credit quality. My EKPC reply affidavit compares that
    methodology with the buyer requirement and explains that, at the same $555/MW-
    day price, the seller posts $121,545 per MW while the buyer posts $1.5 million per
    MW. EKPC Reply Aff. ¶¶ 28–30.

24. I do not suggest that the buyer and seller risks are identical or that the same
    numerical requirement should apply to both. The comparison shows that long-term
    collateral need not be fixed or uniform. PJM’s seller methodology discounts the
    exposure, reflects remaining tenor, and permits reductions that take account of
    credit quality. PJM’s migration analysis does not explain why those variables should
    be omitted from the buyer-side methodology.

25. In my opinion, any additional procedures should permit the buyer-side requirement
    to respond to changes in both the obligor and the exposure over time. A
      requirement intended to address possible future deterioration should not itself
     create a present liquidity stress by ignoring the obligor’s financial capacity.



IV. THE OPT-OUT DISTINCTION DOES NOT TRACK THE RISK IT IS SAID TO
ADDRESS
 26. I addressed the opt-out at paragraphs 12(f), 35, 52 through 57 and 74 of my original
     affidavit and do not repeat that analysis here. PJM’s Answer now explains the
     provision and applies it to another Virginia cooperative. Proposed Tariff,
     Attachment DD, section 18.1(d) permits certain Electric Distributors to elect out of
     the RBP. In its Answer, PJM explains the provision as addressing “a limited
     regulatory gap faced by cooperatives and municipal utilities whose rates are not
     regulated by the states,” on the reasoning that where no state regulatory authority is
     responsible for addressing the reallocation of RBP costs, those utilities’ customers
     are “at risk of absorbing the costs of an ‘overbuy’ if a particular large load fails to
     materialize.” PJM Answer at 30 (citing July 31 Filing, Transmittal Letter at 45).

 27. PJM concludes that the opt-out “should appropriately be limited only to those
     Electric Distributors that are not regulated by the state,” and applies that conclusion
     to Old Dominion Electric Cooperative: because ODEC “is not subject to rate
     regulation by state commissions,” ODEC “would qualify as an Electric Distributor
     that is not subject to regulation by the state and may elect to opt out of the RBP.”
     PJM Answer at 30–31.

 28. NOVEC is a Virginia distribution cooperative whose rates the State Corporation
     Commission regulates. On PJM’s stated criterion, NOVEC is ineligible. Two Virginia
     cooperatives therefore reach opposite results under the same provision.

 29. The distinction does not track the risk. The risk PJM identifies is that utility
     customers may absorb the cost of an overbuy if the forecast large load does not
     materialize. Whether that occurs depends on whether the cost can actually be
     reassigned to the large-load customer and whether the utility can carry the
     obligation in the meantime. State rate regulation does not answer either question. It
     identifies who reviews retail rates; it does not establish a mechanism for
     transferring a fifteen-year wholesale obligation to the customer that caused it.

 30. NOVEC’s exposure to that risk is not reduced by the presence of state rate
     regulation. Its allocation of 1,302.6 RBP UCAP MW derives from a large-load forecast
     submitted for transmission planning purposes, and the filed Tariff provides no
     reconciliation of allocated megawatts against load actually realized. NOVEC Coscia
     Aff. ¶¶ 9(c), 20–22. The overbuy risk PJM describes therefore applies to NOVEC in
     the same form.
 31. In my opinion, the economic rationale for the opt-out would be stronger if eligibility
     tracked the overbuy risk PJM identifies rather than state rate-regulatory status
     standing alone.
 V. THE CONTROLLING MEGAWATT QUANTITY REMAINS UNDEFINED
 32. PJM states in footnote 234 of its Answer that no collateral would be required for
     RBP Resources that are not in service for a Delivery Year and that no RBP Charges
     would be assessed for those resources. PJM Answer at 78 n.234. NOVEC’s answer
     appropriately asks that this interpretation be reflected in the Tariff.
 33. This is not only a drafting issue. Proposed Tariff, Attachment DD, section
     18.8(b)(i)(A) defines the quantity to which the Credit Rate applies by reference to
     “RBP UCAP MW committed”: commitments received through the RBP minus
     commitments rescinded under section 18.6(e). The provision does not state an in-
     service limitation.

 34. That distinction matters because rescission does not occur immediately when a
     resource fails to enter service. As explained in my EKPC reply affidavit, section
     18.6(e) permits a resource to remain committed for up to three Delivery Years
     before rescission, and PJM’s September 14 implementation example for a resource
     that does not come online continues to show committed MW even while Daily
     Owned MW is zero. EKPC Reply Aff. ¶¶ 37–43.

 35. The filed provisions also use the Final RBP Target in determining individual LSE
     postings. Section 18.8(b)(i)(B)(1) scales reported RBP Obligation MW where the
     reported values do not sum to the fixed Final RBP Target. If the procurement clears
     short of the Final RBP Target, committed MW and the Final RBP Target are different
     quantities. My EKPC reply affidavit explains that PJM has identified both as
     governing in different statements. Id. ¶¶ 44–46.
 36. At the filed Credit Rate, each 100 MW difference changes the aggregate collateral
     amount by $150 million. For NOVEC, whose illustrative allocation already produces
     a $1.954 billion requirement, the quantity definition is therefore economically
     material.
 37. In my opinion, an LSE should be able to calculate its requirement directly from the
     Tariff. If PJM intends collateral to follow only in-service MW, that should be stated
     expressly. The Tariff should also establish the relationship among committed MW,
     in-service MW, RBP Obligation MW allocated to an LSE, and the Final RBP Target.



VI. PJM’S PEAK MARKET ACTIVITY CLARIFICATION DOES NOT RESOLVE THE
CREDIT QUESTION
 38. My original NOVEC affidavit stated that once RBP Charges were billed, the same
     economic activity would also enter Peak Market Activity under Attachment Q,
     creating an overlap between the new RBP requirement and existing credit
     treatment. NOVEC Coscia Aff. ¶¶ 10(d), 25–29. PJM has now responded directly to
     that issue.
 39. PJM consents to deleting the proposed sentence stating that settlement of RBP
    positions “may be included, as appropriate, in Peak Market Activity,” because that
    sentence could create confusion that RBP Charges may be captured in Peak Market
    Activity. PJM Answer at 86 n.259. In light of that consent, I do not rest my opinion on
    the proposition that an invoiced RBP Charge would itself be collateralized again
    through Peak Market Activity. The remaining issue is PJM’s treatment of the forward
    RPM component, addressed below.

40. PJM’s new explanation raises a different issue. PJM states that the separate RBP
    requirement must secure the forward RPM component as well as the contract-for-
    differences component, because Peak Market Activity does not prospectively
    collateralize the RPM component over the fifteen-year commitment. PJM Answer at
    87.

41. The relevant comparison is not PJM’s stated rationale but the ordinary treatment of
    the RPM component PJM invokes. Every LSE carries, as a matter of course, a forward
    RPM capacity obligation extending roughly three years. PJM applies its ordinary
    Attachment Q credit framework to that obligation; it does not require collateral
    equal to the full three-year forward RPM payment stream.

42. Consider an RBP commitment with three Delivery Years remaining at an RBP
    commitment price of $555/MW-day and an RPM clearing price of $554/MW-day.
    The forward RPM exposure then has the same horizon as an ordinary capacity
    obligation. Per MW, the contract-for-differences amount over those three years is
    $1,095, while the remaining gross payment stream is $607,725. Applied to NOVEC’s
    illustrative 1,302.6 MW allocation, the three-year contract-for-differences amount is
    approximately $1.43 million, while the total remaining payment stream is
    approximately $791.6 million.
43. PJM’s own roll-off illustration shows the collateral it would hold at that point. At
    three Delivery Years remaining, PJM’s schedule sets collateral equal to the total
    remaining payment obligation: $60,772,500 per 100 MW, or $607,725 per MW.
    September 14 Presentation at 69. Applied to NOVEC’s illustrative allocation, that is
    approximately $791.6 million.

44. At three years remaining, therefore, an ordinary LSE and an RBP buyer carry
    forward RPM obligations of the same horizon at essentially the same price. The
    ordinary obligation remains subject to PJM’s ordinary Attachment Q credit
    treatment. Under PJM’s illustration, the RBP obligation carries collateral equal to
    every remaining dollar of the payment stream. What distinguishes the two is a
    contract for differences of $1/MW-day.

45. In my opinion, the existence of an RBP commitment can justify considering risks not
    present in an ordinary capacity obligation. But at three years remaining the horizon
    is the same, and the RPM exposure is the same. The methodology should explain
    why the credit treatment differs at that point, and how the separate requirement
    converges with ordinary RPM credit treatment as the contract-for-differences
      amount and remaining tenor decline. The answer should not depend solely on
     whether a MW carries the label “RBP.”



VII. PJM’S REDUCTION MECHANISM REMAINS A GROSS-PAYMENT ROLL-OFF,
NOT AN EXPOSURE METHODOLOGY
 46. PJM states that the Credit Rate can decline when previously required collateral
     exceeds remaining expected payment exposure. PJM Answer at 87 & n.261. The
     September 14 Presentation then illustrates a 100 MW obligation at the $1.5 million
     rate.
 47. As described in my EKPC reply affidavit, that illustration holds $150 million of
     collateral unchanged for the first eight Delivery Years. The first reduction occurs in
     the ninth Delivery Year, when the remaining gross payment obligation falls below
     the collateral held. Thereafter, the requirement follows the remaining gross
     payment stream. EKPC Reply Aff. ¶¶ 62–68.

 48. That illustration provides useful information about how PJM presently expects the
     permissive reduction language to operate. The reduction is therefore driven by
     remaining gross payments, not by the RPM clearing price, the contract-for-
     differences amount, participant credit condition, or modeled loss on default.
 49. For NOVEC, a discretionary reduction standard is particularly significant because
     the starting amount is approximately $1.954 billion and the carrying cost is itself
     financially material. NOVEC Coscia Aff. ¶¶ 63–66. A reduction that occurs only after
     remaining gross payments fall below posted collateral can leave the requirement
     unchanged for years despite changes in market prices, remaining tenor, or credit
     condition.

 50. In my opinion, additional procedures should establish objective, tariff-based
     standards for recalculation and release. Those standards should state the frequency
     of review, the inputs used, the circumstances requiring a reduction, and the time
     within which excess collateral is returned.



VIII. A CREDIT DESIGN OF THE KIND NOVEC SEEKS WAS BEFORE PJM IN THE
STAKEHOLDER PROCESS
 51. NOVEC’s answer points to the voluntary, subscription-based framework that
     received sector-weighted supermajority support. On the credit question, that
     framework was specific.

 52. At design component 22.0 of PJM’s package matrix, the package proposed by the
     Joint Electric Distribution Companies and the Data Center Coalition would have used
     a registry to identify, before the procurement, the LSEs required to hold collateral
     and the megawatts for each. It provided that “[i]f an LSE-Large Load cannot post
      collateral, the load is not procured for through the backstop,” and that buyer default
     exposure would be recognized early and funded continuously over time. Package
     Matrix, tab “3. Package Matrix,” design component 22.0.

 53. Two features of that approach bear on the questions addressed above. The obligated
     entity and its megawatt quantity were identified before the procurement rather
     than allocated afterward. And an inability to post operated on the procurement
     rather than on other parties: the megawatts were not bought, and no unsecured
     obligation arose.

 54. PJM states that the Board “adopted various concepts from the Coalition RBP
     Proposal,” identifying the “credit requirement for Load Serving Entities” among
     them. July 31 Filing at 22. The filed construct assigns the obligation to LSEs. It does
     not incorporate the registry, the identification of the obligated entity before the
     procurement, the requirement to post before the obligation attaches, or the
     continuous measurement of exposure as it emerges.
 55. I express no view on whether the Commission should direct adoption of that
     framework. I note only that a credit design addressing the matters identified in this
     affidavit was before PJM and received stakeholder support.



IX. ADDITIONAL PROCEDURES SHOULD ADDRESS THE ENTIRE BUYER-SIDE
CREDIT METHODOLOGY
 56. PJM has consented to Commission resolution of the buyer-side Credit Rate through
     additional procedures and has also stated that the initial rate could be keyed to the
     actual MW-weighted average of selected RBP Sell Offers rather than the maximum
     $555/MW-day. PJM Answer at 92–93.

 57. Using the actual RBP procurement price would reduce the requirement if the
     procurement clears below $555/MW-day. It would not resolve the underlying
     methodology. If the same approximately fifty-percent-of-gross-contractual-value
     approach is applied to a lower price, the number changes but its relationship to
     residual credit exposure remains undefined.

 58. In my opinion, the scope of additional procedures should therefore encompass the
     buyer-side credit framework, not merely the numerical Credit Rate. At a minimum,
     the procedures should determine the residual loss the requirement secures, the
     parties that bear it, and the order in which collateral, section 18.9(a) reallocation,
     and any Operating Agreement section 15.2.2 allocation apply. They should also
     determine the controlling MW quantity, the relationship between RPM payments
     and the contract-for-differences amount, the period of exposure, participant credit
     condition and permissible forms of support, and objective recalculation and release
     standards.
 59. The methodology should then produce the Credit Rate. The reverse approach —
    selecting a collateral amount first and then describing it as a fraction of gross
    contractual value — does not demonstrate that the amount is calibrated to the
    credit loss that can result from default.
60. PJM’s Answer and subsequent implementation materials provide explanations that
    were not available when NOVEC filed its Protest. Those explanations narrow certain
    issues, including the Peak Market Activity issue, but they leave unresolved the
    exposure, quantity, and release mechanics that determine the buyer-side credit
    requirement.

61. For NOVEC, those choices have immediate financial consequences because the filed
    methodology produces an initial requirement of approximately $1.954 billion. In my
    opinion, a requirement of that scale should rest on a defined relationship between
    the amount posted and the loss secured. The present record does not establish that
    relationship.
